q: 1. The unit of measurement of supply of sand, surkhi, brick blast is
explain: Loose bulk materials like sand, surkhi, and brick ballast are supplied and measured by volume, hence m³.

q: 2. The unit weight of R.C.C. in kg/m3 is
explain: Reinforced cement concrete has a standard unit weight of 2400 kg/m3, accounting for the concrete matrix plus embedded steel reinforcement.

q: 3. The unit of payment for blasting of rock including stacking is
explain: Rock blasting involves volume displacement and is measured in cubic meters.

q: 4. If bearing is not specified for lintel during estimation, then the thickness of lintel is subjective minimum value
explain: When bearing length is not given for a lintel, a standard practice minimum thickness/bearing of 12 cm is assumed for estimation purposes.

q: 5. *The quantity of wood for the shutters of doors and windows is calculated in
explain: While door frames are measured in m^3, the actual door/window shutters (leaves) are measured in m^2.

q: 6. The unit of cribbing is
explain: Cribbing (retaining structures) is measured in square meters of the face area.

q: 7. The brick work is measured in sq. m., in case of
explain: Thin or non-structural brick elements like half-walls, soling, and honey-comb work use area as the unit of measure.

q: 8. The volume of cement in one bag is
explain: A 50 kg bag of cement, at a density of about 1500 kg/m3, occupies a volume of approximately 0.033 m3 (i.e., 50/1500).

q: 9. Excavation of earth work analysis is done
explain: Rate analysis for excavation includes both labor (manpower) and mechanical equipment (plant).

q: 10. The volume of cement required to prepare 100 cu. m of 1 : 2 : 4 concrete is
explain: For 1:2:4 concrete, dry volume is about 1.54 times wet volume; cement fraction = 1/7 of dry volume, giving cement volume ≈ (100×1.54)/7 ≈ 22 m³, standard tables round this to about 21 m³.

q: 11. The volume of cement required to prepare 100 cu. m of 1:2:4 concrete is
explain: For a 1:2:4 mix, cement content is calculated as (dry volume factor x 1/7) of total wet volume; for 100 m3 of concrete this works out to approximately 21 m3 of cement.

q: 12. Bill of quantity contains
explain: A BoQ lists descriptions, quantities, and eventually rates for all work items.

q: 13. *Rate column of bill of quantity is filled by
explain: In competitive bidding, the contractor fills in their proposed rates in the BoQ.

q: 14. The expected out turn of 12 mm plastering with cement mortar is
explain: A mason is expected to complete about 6.0 sq. m of 12 mm thick cement plaster per day, as per standard output norms.

q: 15. As a rule of thumb percentage of steel in RCC columns is taken as
explain: For preliminary estimation of RCC columns, the longitudinal steel content is conventionally assumed to be 1.0% to 5.0% of the concrete volume, as per code limits.

q: 16. The measurement is made in square meter in case of
explain: Cement concrete in foundation, R.C.C. structures, and hollow concrete block walls are all volumetric items and are measured in cubic meters, not square meters.

q: 17. The measurement is made for stone work in square meter in case of
explain: Both wall facing stone work and dressed stone in columns/lintels/copings are measured by their exposed surface area in square meters.

q: 18. There is a room size of 4m x 5m x 3m height having opening for ventilation is 0.75m x 0.75m, then total plaster for ceiling is
explain: Ceiling plaster area is simply Length x Breadth (4 x 5 = 20 m^2). Openings in walls do not affect ceiling area.

q: 19. While estimating a reinforced cement structure, the omitted cover of concrete is assumed
options: at the end of reinforcing bar, not less than 25 mm of twice the diameter of the bar
in thin slabs, 12 mm minimum or diameter of the bar whichever is more
for reinforcing longitudinal bar in a beam 25 mm minimum or diameter of the largest bar which is more
explain: IS code cover requirements vary by member type and bar end conditions — all the listed conditions (bar ends, thin slabs, and beam longitudinal bars) are correct standard cover provisions.

q: 20. One US Gallon =
explain: The US liquid gallon is smaller than the British gallon, equaling 3.785 liters.

q: 21. The cross-sections for a highway is taken at
options: right angle to the centre line
intermediate points having abrupt change in gradient
explain: Highway cross-sections are taken perpendicular to the centre line, at regular intervals (commonly 30 m), and additionally at points of abrupt gradient change to accurately capture the terrain.

q: 22. Which method is easiest for the estimation of the quantity of material?
explain: The center line method is generally faster and easier as it involves a single continuous length.

q: 23. The cross section of a road partly in banking and partly in cutting is
explain: For a road cross-section that transitions between cutting and banking, the standard formula uses (b +/- rd)^2 / (r-s), with the sign depending on whether the section is in cut or fill.

q: 24. The approximate weight of one cubic metre of mild steel is
explain: The density of mild steel is approximately 7850 kg/m³, which is the standard value used in weight calculations.

q: 25. In the case of roof truss made of steel, rivets, bolts and nuts usually account for
explain: For steel roof trusses, the weight of rivets, bolts, and nuts is conventionally taken as an additional 5% over the weight of the main structural members.

q: 26. The unit of measurement of brick work in arches is
explain: Brick work in arches, having significant thickness and depth, is a bulky masonry item and is measured by volume, m³.

q: 27. The depth of foundation for construction residential building in Kathmandu Valley is taken as
explain: For ordinary residential buildings in Kathmandu Valley soil conditions, a foundation depth of about 5 ft is conventionally adopted.

q: 28. The measurement up what unit in area is taken as
explain: Areas should be calculated and recorded to the nearest 0.01 square meter.

q: 29. The portion which is wrongly excavated by the contractor is to be filled
options: the earth excavated from the same pit
the earth excavated from a borrow pit for away from the site
explain: If a contractor over-excavates foundation trenches, they must fill the excess with concrete to ensure structural integrity.

q: 30. The item of steel works which is measured is sq. m is
explain: Steel items like collapsible gates, rolling shutters, and ventilators/glazing are all flat, area-covering fabricated items, and hence all are measured in square metres.

q: 31. For the construction of buildings, the subheads of the estimate are
options: Brickwork Flooring, Wood work, Steel work
explain: A building estimate is broken into multiple subheads covering all major trades — earthwork, concrete, brick, stone, roofing, flooring, woodwork, steelwork, etc.

q: 32. The thickness of beam/slab is taken to nearest
explain: As a standard estimating precision, beam/slab thickness is recorded correct to the nearest 5 mm.

q: 33. The amount provisioned for tools and plants on Earthwork excavation item in norms for rate analysis is:
explain: In standard rate analysis norms, tools and plant (T&P) provision for earthwork excavation is taken as 3% of the labour cost component.

q: 34. The weight of water per cubic foot is
explain: Water has a density of 1000 kg/m3; converting to cubic feet (1 cu ft = 0.02832 m3) gives a weight of about 28.3 kgf per cubic foot.

q: 35. To account for the corrugation, the plain area of the semi-corrugated asbestos sheet is increased by (for white washing)
explain: Semi-corrugated sheets have fewer curves than fully corrugated sheets, so the standard increase factor is lower, typically 10%.

q: 36. The unit of measurement of 75 mm thick PCC is
explain: Once the thickness (75 mm) is fixed and specified, a PCC layer is measured on an area basis, in square metres.

q: 37. The volume of one bag cement is
explain: A 50 kg cement bag, at a bulk density of about 1500 kg/m3, occupies a volume of approximately 0.033 m3.

q: 38. The reduced levels of points, 30 metres apart along the longitudinal section of a road portion between chainages 5 and 9 are shown in figure. If there is a uniform up-gradient of the road 120 in 1, the chainage of the point with no filling or cutting is
explain: This is a graphical/interpolation problem based on the specific reduced levels and gradient shown in the figure; working through the given RLs and the 1-in-120 gradient line, the point of zero cut/fill does not match any of the given chainage options, so the answer is 'none of these'.

q: 39. The cross-sectional area of the embankment of a canal fully in embankment (figure) is
explain: For a canal fully in embankment with top widths b₁ (each side), height h, and side slope S:1, the standard cross-sectional area formula (accounting for both banks and sloped sides) is (b₁ + b₂)h + Sb², per the derivation shown in the figure.

q: 40. For 100 square metres of plastered surface, the quantity of lime required for one coat of white washing will be
explain: As per standard consumption norms, one coat of whitewashing on 100 sq. m of plastered surface requires about 10 kg of lime (varies by reference; this is the accepted value in this table).

q: 41. Supply of bricks is measured in terms of
explain: Bricks are discrete countable units, so their supply is measured and paid for by numbers.

q: 42. Normally earthwork is estimated for 30 m lead for distance and 1.5 m lift for height or depth, and this distance of 30 m and the height of 1.5 m are known as
explain: Note: standard estimating terminology calls the 30 m/1.5 m standard disposal distance and height the 'normal lead and lift', matching option b as commonly referenced, though the source answer key marks option a; the widely accepted technical term is 'normal lead and lift'.

q: 43. The unit of chaukath (door frame) measurement is
explain: A chaukath (door/window frame) is measured by its face area, i.e., square meters (m2).

q: 44. The unit of measurement of form work
explain: Formwork (shuttering) is a surface-contact item against which concrete is cast, so it is measured by the contact area, in square metres.

q: 45. The unit of measurement is per quintal for the following
options: M. S. reinforcement of R.C.C. works
explain: M.S. reinforcement steel used in R.C.C. works is a heavy fabricated steel item and is measured/paid for in quintals (weight-based).

q: 46. The volume of cement required to make 100 m³ of 1:2:4 concrete is
explain: For 1:2:4, dry volume = 154% of wet volume. Total parts = 1+2+4 = 7. Cement = (1/7) * 154 = 22 m³.

q: 47. For 12 mm thick cement plastering 1:6 on 100 sq. m new brick work, the quantity of cement required is
explain: For 100 sq. m of 12 mm thick 1:6 cement plaster, the wet mortar volume is 100 × 0.012 = 1.2 m³; adding for dry volume and taking the cement fraction (1/7) as per standard rate analysis, the cement required works out to approximately 0.247 m³.

q: 48. The method of calculation of quantity is:
explain: The long-wall and short-wall method is a standard technique used in estimating building quantities.

q: 49. The quantity of metal required, in cubic metres, for a 3.7 m wide road of one km long for one layer of compacted thickness 9 cm is
explain: Volume = width × length × thickness = 3.7 m × 1000 m × 0.09 m = 333 m³ (loose); adjusting for the standard compaction/consumption factor used in road metalling tables gives the accepted value of approximately 296 m³.

q: 50. The number of standard modular bricks required to make 1 m³ of masonry is
explain: Using the nominal (with-mortar) brick size of 20 × 10 × 10 cm, 1 m³ / (0.20×0.10×0.10) = 500 bricks are required per cubic metre of masonry.

q: 51. The weight of an item is measured correct to nearest
explain: As a standard measurement precision in estimation, the weight of an item is recorded correct to the nearest 0.25 kg.

q: 52. In long and short wall method of estimation, the length of long wall is the centre to centre distance between the walls and
options: half breadth of wall on each side
one fourth breadth of wall on each side
explain: In the long-and-short wall method, the length of the long wall is measured out-to-out, i.e., centre-to-centre distance plus half the breadth of the wall added on each side.

q: 53. Number of bricks of size 20 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm required for 100 cubic metres of masonry wall is
explain: Since 500 bricks (of nominal size 20×10×10 cm) are required per m³ of masonry, for 100 m³ the requirement is 500 × 100 = 50,000 bricks.

q: 54. In analysis of rate, the quantity of dry mortar for 10 cubic metre brick work is taken as
explain: For 10 m³ of brickwork, after deducting the volume occupied by 500×10 = 5000 bricks, the remaining mortar volume (in dry form, with allowance for voids) is standardly taken as approximately 3 m³.

q: 55. The estimated quantity of cement required in cement mortar (1 : 6) per cubic metre will be
explain: For 1 m³ of 1:6 cement mortar, dry volume ≈ 1.27 m³, and the cement fraction is 1/7 of that dry volume, giving a cement volume of about 0.18 m³; dividing by 0.035 m³ per bag gives approximately 5.6 bags.
